content.thinking:
I'm planning out a chunky Blizzard-style dwarf rifleman model, around 1.3m tall with a braided beard and blunderbuss, and setting up the builder structure and imports needed to construct it carefully in one pass.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton coordinates—short thick legs, big head and shoulders, oversized hands—working out joint positions for hips, spine, neck, and head, then starting the leg IK chain with hip, knee, and ankle targets and bend directions.

Adding more rig joints...

Using absolute world coordinates instead, where s=1 corresponds to +X/left, and naming each side "L" or "R" accordingly. I'm now laying out the spine chain as a catmull curve from the hips joint upward through several points toward the upper torso, assigning names like "spine1", "spine2" etc. to each segment.

I'm sketching the overall dwarf proportions: a broad barrel torso roughly from hip to shoulder height, a large head with a sizable radius, a helmet peak, and a total standing height around 1.3 units, which feels about right for a stocky dwarf. Now I'm defining a short neck chain connecting the torso to the head joint with appropriate parenting.

Still defining joints...

For the torso itself, I'm planning to sweep an elliptical cross-section along the spine chain, with the radius varying by position to create a barrel shape, shifting the belly forward slightly.

Continuing the radii profile, I'm adjusting shoulders and tapering down to the neck, then using a shift function to push the belly slightly forward along the z-axis so the torso silhouette reads naturally from the side.

I'm adding a hip sphere scaled flatter in the depth and height axes to round out the pelvis, then setting up the arm joint chain -- shoulder, elbow, wrist, hand tip -- positioned under the chest for a dwarf with oversized pauldrons, keeping the rest pose neutral and readable as described in the guide.

For the blunderbuss pose, I'm thinking through a simple carrying stance: maybe the left arm bends to grip the fore stock while the right arm holds the weapon lower at the hip, avoiding a complicated "port arms" setup that would be hard for IK to read cleanly.

I'm settling on a compromise rest pose: right arm bent holding the blunderbuss at the hip with the barrel angled up and forward around 35°, left arm relaxed to balance the stance for easier rigging.

For fingers I'll simplify to a thumb joint plus a curled fingers joint per hand, with the right hand's fingers wrapped around the gun grip. I'm reconsidering the arm pose though—rather than bending the elbow forward to carry the gun at hip level, maybe it's cleaner to let the arm hang straight down with the gun held vertically, butt resting near the ground, keeping the A-pose naturally relaxed.

Actually, simpler to just have him carry the gun diagonally at the hip, muzzle pointing up-forward, rather than straight vertical — that reads more naturally as a held weapon.

I'm computing the gun's orientation vector tilted up and inward, then working through the right arm's joint positions—shoulder, elbow, and wrist—to figure out where the hand grips the weapon.

I'll settle on an elbow bend hint pointing outward-back so the elbow lands roughly behind and slightly below the shoulder. Then I'm placing the gun axis in absolute coordinates relative to the hand position, defining it as a parametric line through the grip with the butt behind the hand and the muzzle extending forward, totaling about 0.86 in length with a flared end.

Checking the butt position against the elbow location, I'm noticing a collision — the stock overlaps the elbow area, so I need to shorten the stock or shift the gun axis outward to avoid the arm, repositioning the butt closer to the hip instead.

Checking the butt position puts it just below the forearm with a slight gap, which works fine tucked beneath it. The gun direction vector normalizes out cleanly at roughly (0.08, 0.57, 0.82), so I'm good to compute the muzzle position next.

The muzzle at the far end lands at about (-0.256, 1.05, 0.72), roughly chin height but far enough forward to clear the head — this reads as a blunderbuss held upward at 35°, a nice "ready" pose. Now I'm considering the left arm: it could rest relaxed in an A-pose, or grip the foregrip of the gun partway along its length, which would mean crossing the arm over the chest from the left shoulder toward that forward point.

Checking the distance for that reach, it's too far for a natural arm length, so instead I'm leaning toward keeping the left arm in a relaxed A-pose with a slight elbow bend and an open hand — maybe holding nothing, or possibly adding a small prop like a powder flask, pouch, or bandolier for visual interest rather than forcing an unnatural pose.

Defining tapered radius values for the arm using a smooth gradient from shoulder to wrist, building the chain with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints, and planning leather bracer coloring for the dwarf's sleeves.

Now I'm settling on the costume palette: ruddy tan skin with darker shadow tones, a fiery copper-red beard and hair with gold rings and braided beads, and Ironforge-blue armor accented with gold trim, dark steel, brown leather, and cream cloth.

I'm capping the palette around 30 flat colors and planning a shading helper that mixes a base color with highlight and shadow tones based on surface normal, to give that hand-painted top-lit look.

Adding noise mottling and grain patterns...

For the head I'll keep it simple with the lit() helper plus mottled grain, skipping separate decals for nose/cheek flush. Now I'm planning the beard as a swept/looped tube mass with hair-strand grain running along the vertical axis to simulate braided copper-to-light-copper streaks.

For the moustache I'll curve two swept tubes outward from the upper lip with spiraled tips, and for the side braids I'll chain small alternating ellipsoid beads along a path to fake a plaited look, finishing each with a gold ring clasp and tassel tip. I'm budgeting part counts carefully (roughly 14 beads per braid, times two, plus the beard mass) to stay under the 1000-part limit, and I'm adding dedicated "beardL"/"beardR" joint bones so the beard rides naturally with the head and jaw.

Writing braid chain logic...

I'm thinking I can get a better braid look by using an oscillating radius along the sweep to create lumps, combined with a spiral stripe paint pattern for the chevron effect — simpler than complex chevron math but still reads clearly as braided. I'll also toss in a gold torus ring part at the tie point for a finishing detail.

Actually a true three-strand plait could work better: compute three helical offset paths around a shared centerline, each strand a short catmull curve with overlapping radius so they visually interlock into a chunky braid, riding along the bone chain for smooth skinning.

Now I'm turning to the beard itself — a large dwarven beard covering the chest, lofted from the jawline downward with stations widening then tapering to a point, figuring out how the cross-section width and depth should orient relative to the downward path direction.

I'm thinking through how to attach the beard: whether it should rigidly follow the head bone or hang from a dedicated chain tied to the chin, since parts near the chest would look odd rigid on the head. I'm leaning toward a small "beard" bone chain starting near the chin for smoother sweep deformation.

Now I'm defining the beard geometry stations with position, width, and height values to loft a tapering tail shape, trying to reuse the same points for both the bone chain and the loft curve so they stay aligned.

I'm checking the beard's length and depth relative to the torso — making sure the tip falls above the belt and that the beard's front surface clears the chest without clipping, which means I need to nudge the torso's chest depth slightly inward.

Now I'm placing the head itself: a wide-jawed dwarf skull with a heavy brow ridge, bulbous reddish nose, full cheeks, and small eyes tucked under the brow.

For the helmet I'm thinking a brass-trimmed Ironforge-style steel cap with a gold band, rivets, and a small crest ridge instead of a nose guard so the face stays visible. I'll add brass-rimmed gunner goggles pushed up on the forehead strap for that dwarven engineer feel.

For the face, I'm separating the lower jaw from the upper skull so the beard and moustache naturally cover the mouth, with just a dark slit hinting at the mouth underneath. I considered adding a little pipe at the corner of the mouth for character but decided to skip it to keep things simple.

I'll keep my toolkit minimal and reliable since I can't test iteratively: basic geometries, sweeps, rods, lathes, and extrudes, avoiding riskier features like decals or sticks. For any emblem, I'll design my own original heraldry rather than referencing any existing logos or characters.

I'll apply SVG textures onto plane geometries for details like a chest emblem, belt buckle, and trim embroidery, making sure the planes face outward correctly and using white as the base color so the texture's own colors show through properly. Now I want to nail down precise measurements before writing the actual code.

Defining the color palette...

Defining the neck, head, and jaw joints with their parent relationships and aim targets, placing the jaw hinge near the ears and aiming toward the chin.

Now I'm sketching the skull geometry: an ellipsoid head center with specific radii, figuring out the lower jaw sphere position, and working out where the eyes sit relative to the skull surface using the ellipsoid equation.

I'm also placing small embedded eye spheres with white sclera and dark irises, then positioning angled brow capsules above them that slant down toward the nose to give a gruff, angry look.

Now I'm shaping the nose as a flattened, flushed sphere with a bridge capsule connecting it to the brow, adding puffy flushed cheeks, and sketching out small pointed ears positioned to be mostly tucked under the helmet.

I'm working out the jawline shape hidden beneath the beard, then routing sideburn tubes from the ears down along the jaw to blend into the beard mass, with the moustache planned as thick curved tubes meeting beneath the nose.

I'll rig the moustache to the head bone since it sits above the mouth, letting it move naturally with the jaw. For the mouth itself, I'll skip adding a visible dark slit since it'd mostly be hidden beneath the moustache and beard anyway—not worth the wasted geometry.

Thinking more about the beard: since it hangs below the chin, I should parent its chain to the jaw bone rather than the head, so it swings naturally with jaw movement. The chain root sits near y=1.1, close to where the jaw bone starts, which makes this parenting choice sensible—though I won't worry about perfectly matching up the chin skin color between moustache and beard since there will be some natural overlap there.

I'm working out the forward offsets so the moustache slightly overlaps the top of the beard, covering the mouth seam, and nudging the beard's starting position forward to close that gap. For the neck I'm adding a short rigid cylinder bone with skin material, plus a gold-trimmed blue collar piece to sit around it.

For torso clothing, I'm planning a body sweep painted with banded colors—trousers below the hip, blue tunic above—and adding a torus/sweep belt shape around the waist at the hip line.

Generating belt ellipse points...

I'm considering using a lathe for belt-like bands, scaling the mesh elliptically to match the torso shape, but worrying lathe options might not support scale directly—so I may fall back to a cylinder geometry for the belt instead.

So the belt band becomes a solid scaled cylinder sized slightly larger than the torso radius, positioned at the belt height. Since nearest-joint attachment could grab the wrong bone, I should explicitly pass the bone (like spine1) along with the `at` position so placement stays precise.

I'm defining a small `put` helper that wraps `b.part` with explicit bone, position, and options, then I need to sort out typing for the color parameter -- checking whether `Fill` or `ColorInput` from the paint module is the right type to accept both strings and `Paint` instances safely.

Defining helper closures for part placement and geometry shortcuts...

Adding boot details...

I'll just rely on the ankle tip joint rather than adding a separate toe joint, keeping the rig simpler. I'm checking that the sole box and foot ball both touch the ground plane exactly, with a small sink allowance for visual grounding, and now I'm placing knee pad plates using the knee joint position from the limb computation.

For the legs, I'm estimating hip-to-ankle distance against the thigh and shin segment lengths, bending the knee forward with a small offset to satisfy the triangle inequality, and tapering the leg radius from thigh to ankle for a tapered silhouette.

I'm sweeping the leg as a polyline with a smooth fillet at the knee, using evenly spaced radius keys along the chain. For the torso, I'm filling the pelvis with a scaled ball joining the hips, colored as trousers, and adding a hanging tasset flap of cloth in front of the crotch down to the hem.

For the tabard, I'm planning front and back cloth panels with a painted trim, using the box's UV coordinates per face to generate a gold border near the bottom edge and side seams—a simple trick that works for any box or plane since the UV space is shared across faces.

Given a texture around 1024 texels covering roughly 4 square meters of painted surface, I'm estimating texel density to confirm it's fine enough (around 2.4mm per texel), then sketching out an SVG design for the tabard front: blue cloth with gold border, stitched detail lines, and a central emblem featuring a gold sunburst or shield motif.

I'm planning the emblem as a mountain peak with a sun, cutting the tabard's bottom hem into a swallowtail shape via an alpha-masked polygon outline, and adding a second plain-blue plane on the back so the garment doesn't look hollow from behind. For the remaining gear I'm sketching simpler approaches: a gold buckle built as geometry rather than texture, a bandolier with painted shot pouches, and wood-grain/brass detailing on the gun using procedural paint techniques.

For the arms, I'm deciding on blue short sleeves to the elbow with bare, skin-toned forearms wrapped in a studded leather or steel vambrace, using a color-band function along the arm's path that transitions from sleeve color to skin color at roughly the elbow point, plus small gold rune markings on the pauldron and an emblem on the pouch flap.

Now I'm working out the hands: a palm box with four finger capsules and a separate thumb joint, parented to the wrist for grouping, positioning the left hand's wrist coordinates and figuring the arm direction from elbow to wrist to orient the fingers naturally.

Positioning fingers along world X for the four digits, then building each as a two-segment capsule for curl...

Still writing finger sweep geometry... Now figuring out thumb placement, offsetting from the palm edge with the correct inward direction and forward orientation for a relaxed A-pose hand.

For the right hand gripping the gun, I'm approximating a fist by combining a central block with curled knuckle spheres and a thumb capsule layered over the grip, stacking segments to simulate wrapped fingers.

Working out the finger wrap geometry: the fist spans about 0.11 wide, with fingers as capsule rods running along world X, curling from the palm side on the right across to the fingertip side on the left, crossing the grip's underside roughly in the plane perpendicular to the grip axis.

Now I'm working out the gun's geometry, designing it as a chunky blunderbuss-style barrel aligned along its own axis, using cylinders oriented along that direction so the parts stay consistent with the gun's tilt.

Working out the default aim orientation: with no explicit up vector, the local X axis stays near world -X and local Z becomes the cross product of X and the direction vector, which gives me a usable perpendicular "up" direction for positioning the box parts correctly.

Tracing through the basis construction more carefully: s is derived as the perpendicular component of d crossed with a fixed X0=(1,0,0), then the local right vector comes from crossing d with s. I'm working out the cross product components explicitly to pin down the exact orientation.

Now I'm starting to lay out the gun's actual geometry in gun-frame coordinates, placing the grip at s=0 and defining the stock as a tapering shape from the butt forward.

Continuing the taper into the wrist, then placing a brass butt plate box oriented to the stock's direction. I'm also thinking through the lock plate placement on the visible side of the gun — figuring out which lateral side faces the viewer so the engraved steel side plate reads correctly.

I'm now mapping out the hammer as a curved swept shape rising above the lock, then sweeping the brass trigger guard loop below the grip with a small trigger rod inside it, before moving on to shape the flared barrel.

For the barrel, I'm using a lathe profile narrow near the breech and widening into a bell shape toward the muzzle, defining radius-height pairs along the axis to build that blunderbuss flare.

Still defining barrel geometry...

I'll place the cone top slightly above the rim face so only a thin dark disc peeks through, then add a thin gold-trim torus ring around the muzzle lip for highlight. For decoration I'm thinking of adding brass bands along the barrel and a trim ring near the bell flare, possibly using the lathe's paint function to color sections by height rather than separate geometry.

Now I'm adding a wood fore-stock under the barrel, a thin brass-tipped ramrod with brass retaining rings, and considering a leather bandolier strap across the dwarf's chest instead of a sling on the gun itself, plus a small brass flintlock pan box at the lock mechanism.

I'm wiring up the gun joint so it parents to the wrist joint of the right arm chain, aiming toward a target point, with fingers and thumb joints also attaching at the wrist, then moving on to counting out the full joint list starting from hips and spine.

Tallying up the rest of the skeleton (neck, head, jaw, legs, arms, fingers, gun, braids, beard) lands me around 35 joints, which feels workable. Now I'm planning the hanging accessories—a tapered powder horn on the left hip with a brass cap and strap, a leather ammo pouch at the right hip, and a diagonal bandolier strap running from the right shoulder.

For the bandolier I need it to hug the torso's actual surface rather than guess, so I'm deriving an analytic torso radius function from the spine's catmull points and interpolated rx/ry values instead of relying on a drape API I'm unsure of — trusting explicit geometry over an uncertain shortcut.

I'm approximating z-offset as a roughly linear function of y, giving a close fit to the target depth values at the key points.

Now I realize the normal direction runs symmetrically forward and back, so to get a cute potbelly look I need to shift the center point slightly forward rather than keeping it symmetric, while making the belly radius bigger than the chest radius.

Defining spine points...

I'm setting up a helper that interpolates torso radii along the height, then planning the bandolier's shell cylinders—small brass-and-red cartridges spaced along the strap, each built as separate parts oriented along the strap direction rather than merged geometry.

For the pauldrons, I'm shaping steel-and-gold shoulder domes using partial hemisphere spheres (open underside, hidden by the arms), tilted outward and offset above each shoulder joint.

Working out the sign convention for rotating the dome outward on each side, then layering three stepped overlapping plates to mimic lame armor.

I'm computing the gold trim torus at the dome's rim intersection, adding small rivet spheres around the edge, and considering a small spike cone on top. I'm also thinking about whether to keep the pauldrons symmetric or add asymmetric detail, and starting to plan the helmet's lathe profile with a brass brim.

Working out the helmet's exact dimensions now — checking the radius profile points against the skull sphere's position so the helmet dome clears the skull with a small gap at the top, and verifying the front brim doesn't clip into the brow geometry.

With helmet base at 1.215 and height 0.14, the top lands around 1.355, and with a small crest or gold knob the total comes to roughly 1.38-1.40m, which is reasonable for a dwarf proportion.

Now I'm checking the face visibility: with eyes at y=1.17 and brow at 1.205 sitting just under the helmet brim at 1.215, the forehead stays hidden while eyes, nose, and brow remain exposed between helmet and beard. I'm adjusting the helmet's z-position slightly forward so the brow juts out naturally under the brim, keeping the back aligned with the skull extending toward the hair and neck area.

I'm also planning a copper hair mass at the back under the helmet, plus a small decorative crest fin running along the top of the helmet from front to back, shaped as an extruded profile following the dome's curve.

Still defining the sweep path...

I'm recalculating the crest path so it sits just above the dome surface rather than embedded in it, interpolating the dome's y-values at each radius and adding a small offset to get the final crest coordinates.

I'm nudging the crest height down slightly so the overall helmet tops out around 1.39, deciding not to rescale the whole model and instead accept this proportion. Now I'm planning rivet details along the brim, spacing small gold spheres evenly around the circumference using an angular loop.

Next I'm figuring out the goggles: a leather strap torus tilted around the helmet near the dome, with two brass lens cylinders angled forward-up and positioned symmetrically on the front dome surface, working out their exact placement coordinates based on the dome's curvature.

I'll add a brass goggle frame torus and a leather strap band around the helmet with a brass buckle, then move to the chest design — a blue cloth tunic with a steel breastplate layered over the torso.

Actually that sector approach won't work since uncovered angles still render in piece colour, covering the whole tube. Let me try a different approach instead: using a scaled, partially-angled sphere as an ellipsoid breastplate that sits mostly buried in the torso but protrudes at the front chest.

Checking the dimensions, the breastplate ellipsoid fits without poking through the sides and gives a modest 5cm front plate. But I realize the dwarf's beard hangs down over most of the chest area anyway, so the breastplate detail will largely be hidden underneath it regardless.

Given that, I'll shorten the beard tip so the belt and tabard remain visible below it, and add braids hanging from the beard sides down past the belt line. The breastplate will still peek out at the sides where the beard doesn't cover, so I'll keep its width. Then I'm planning a front tabard panel running from the belt down to the hem.

I'll make it a thin box rotated slightly about the X axis so the bottom edge tilts outward and forward, with a small negative angle so the top stays tucked back near the belt.

Actually, using the `dir`/`axis` approach is simpler: setting the local +Z along a tilt direction with up aligned to world +Y keeps the drawing upright while the panel leans. The front panel's normal should point forward-and-up (bottom forward, top back), while the back panel's normal points backward-and-up correspondingly.

For the tabard texture, I'll design an SVG swallowtail shape with a gold border, a cream center stripe, and a sun emblem, using a subtle gradient for painted-highlight shading, sized to a 100:140 aspect ratio and scaled to fit the tabard plane dimensions.

I'm skipping separate pauldron plates since curved-dome alignment is tricky, and instead painting the pauldron directly with procedural radial gold ribs against a steel base, using UV coordinates on the sphere geometry -- this avoids placement risk entirely and I might add a trim ring near the rim too.

For hands and arms, I'm going with bare skin on the hands but adding leather bracers with gold studs on the forearms, plus a steel vambrace on the left arm. I'm orienting these forearm cylinders using the actual limb direction vector so they align naturally along the arm, scaling the radius to match the arm's thickness at that point.

Now I'm working through the shoulder joint placement -- the arm attaches outside the torso edge near the pauldron, so I need a rounded cap sphere at the shoulder to blend the upper arm tube smoothly into the body surface without a visible gap.

For the arms, I'm setting up both limb chains: left shoulder near (0.28, 0.93, 0) reaching toward a wrist target around (0.42, 0.43, 0.07), and the mirrored right arm with shoulder at (-0.28, 0.93, 0) and wrist near (-0.3, 0.74, 0.22), picking bend-direction hints so the elbows angle back and outward in a natural pose.

Still solving elbow geometry...

That gives elbow at roughly (-0.39, 0.72, -0.02), with the upper arm extending outward and down while the forearm curves forward and inward toward x=-0.3 — a natural bent-arm pose. Now shifting to the left arm, I'm computing the shoulder-to-wrist distance vector to figure out its length.

Checking the gun butt position relative to the torso — it clears the body by about 12cm on the right side, sitting close to but just below the elbow, which looks fine.

Verifying the muzzle position stays clear of the dwarf's head, and that the overall gun length (~0.87m) is oversized but fits the chunky Warcraft aesthetic for an oversized weapon. I'm also checking the left hand placement near the thigh clears the leg surface, and deciding no sling or strap is needed.

I'll skip the glowing fuse/ember idea since magic glow isn't typical for this dwarf design, instead just glowing the goggle lenses. I'm adding a rucksack with a bedroll and tin cup on the back for extra silhouette and storytelling detail, positioning the pack box and bedroll cylinder across the back near the bone chest area.

Writing strap geometry...

The shoulder strap positioning is getting too fiddly to compute precisely against the sloped torso geometry, and the pauldron would hide that area anyway, so I'll skip shoulder straps entirely and just render the pack straps as simple lines across the back.

Working out the pack box placement is tricky since it keeps overlapping the torso's back curve slightly depending on where I set its z-center and depth—I'm nudging the position until the front face of the pack clears the torso back by just a hair.

Now I'm figuring out the rest of the pack: a tilted flap on top, two side pouches, strap boxes, gold buckles, and a bedroll cylinder resting on top sized and positioned to sit flush against the pack's upper edge, rotated so it runs sideways. I'm adding red-and-cream striping along the bedroll's length so the rolled blanket shows alternating bands, then adding leather strap boxes wrapped around it to hold it in place.

I'm adding a hanging tin cup near the pack's side, skipping extra items like a frying pan, lantern, map tube, cape, or scarf. Then I'm working out hip gear placement -- moving a pouch from the right hip to the back-right to avoid colliding with the gun butt, sizing it appropriately, and adding a powder horn on the left hip with a hanging cord.

Now I'm placing a small hatchet on the left hip, hanging from the belt with its handle running vertically along the thigh and the axe head pointing downward, defining the wedge-shaped blade outline...

Adding the handle and head placement details...

I'm placing the hatchet handle at x=.25, checking it clears the thigh outline, and figuring out where to attach it via a belt loop strap. For the powder horn, I'm deciding to hang it on the left hip bandolier instead, around (0.19, 0.6, 0.14), since the hatchet already occupies the right side.

Now I'm defining the horn's curved path with tapering radii and cream coloring plus a brass cap at the wide end, then checking it doesn't collide with the hatchet handle by comparing their z-depths—separated enough to be safe. I'm also verifying the bandolier end position sits near the horn without overlap, and starting to check whether the tabard fabric might clip into the hatchet.

Moving on to clothing layers, I decide to skip extra waist plates and faulds since the tabard covers that area adequately, and settle on brown trousers, tall boots with turned-down cuffs and gold buckles, plus steel knee guards. Now I'm working out the beard braids—placing their roots at the lower sides of the beard and tracing a curved path down the chest, cross-checking the beard's width and curvature at various heights to make sure the braids sit naturally against it.

I refine the beard profile into clean stations with width and height values tapering from wide near the chin to a narrow pointed end lower down, giving it that forked Warcraft-style look before the braids take over. Then I work out the surface depth at the braid attachment point so the braids sit flush against the beard's curved front.

For the beard chain, I set up a catmull-rom path through the six beard points, parented to the jaw bone, with five named segments matching the five spans so there's no dangling tip bone. For shading, I plan to build a fur-like paint function combining grain-based strand texture with a vertical gradient that darkens toward the roots and lightens toward the tips.

Writing noise-based strand shader...

Skin uses a lit shader with subtle grain, while gold and small details stick to flat colors to stay within the palette budget, reserving painted shading for larger surfaces. Now I'm setting up the steel armor paint...

Steel gets a lit shader with scratches, blue cloth follows a similar lit approach with minor weave texture, and leather uses grain at a lower intensity. Checking the painted area budget confirms it fits within the shared texture sheet, so I'm moving on to placing face details like the eye spheres positioned relative to the skull geometry.

Working out iris and pupil placement at the right z-depth so they're visible beyond the white sphere, then building the eyelid as a scaled half-sphere to cover the top of the eye.

I'll keep the dwarf's eyes small and deep-set, with the jaw built as a scaled sphere hidden mostly by the beard, and skip extra details like under-eye bags or visible teeth since the moustache covers the mouth area.

Now I'm adding ears with pointed tips using small cones, plus gold ring earrings made from rotated torus shapes at the lobes, and building a hair mass behind the head using a scaled sphere positioned to suggest beard-colored strands.

Sideburns extend from the hair as curved paths connecting to the beard, using radius-tapered tube segments. I'm skipping scars and freckles, keeping the neck mostly hidden by the beard, and adding a steel gorget collar as a torus ring positioned at the neck base.

For the pauldron, I'm deciding whether it should attach to the chest/clavicle for stability or the shoulder joint so it moves with arm rotation -- I'll go with chest attachment for simplicity. Now I'm figuring out placement for the belt buckle, calculating the front z-coordinate based on the belt cylinder's scale factor to position a gold buckle plate correctly against the body.

Then I'm working out stud placement around the belt, computing x/z positions using sine and cosine of angles spanning roughly -70° to 70° at the belt's radius to scatter nine small gold spheres while skipping the buckle position at the center, before moving on to wrist cuffs and setting up a finger joint bone chain parented to the wrist with aim direction toward the knuckle.

I need the radius function to return a tuple shape, so I should make sure the arrow function's return value is explicitly typed as a two-number tuple rather than letting TypeScript infer a generic array.

For the torso, I'm writing a helper that linearly interpolates between keyframe rows indexed by a y-value, pulling out radius and depth parameters at each key point...

Now I'm recalculating the belt geometry, adjusting its radius to 0.225 and scaling it on the z-axis to around 0.76 so the band fits correctly outside the torso surface at that height.

I'm checking the torso radius interpolates from the key values across t, with a cap overlapping the pelvis smoothly. For coloring, I'm considering banding by t—pants hue near the hem, transitioning to a blue tunic higher up, possibly with a leather-toned lower band.

Working out the tunic hem and gold trim ring dimensions so they sit cleanly where the torso meets the pelvis sphere, since the pelvis ellipsoid is wider than the torso at that junction.

I'm settling on scaled-down pelvis dimensions so the pants peek below the tunic hem naturally, and now deciding on the color palette: blue tunic, brownish leather pants, steel accents, and copper beard.

Now I'm working out boot and chest plate details, then positioning a tabard plane hanging from the belt to cover the crotch area, computing coordinates based on the pelvis and hip geometry.

I'm checking that the tabard tucks under the belt's solid cylinder so it doesn't clip visibly, then verifying the tabard's bottom edge hangs properly in front of the thighs without intersecting them.

But at 9cm it floats too far from the thighs, so I'm tilting the plane so the bottom edge angles in toward the legs, slanting the top forward by about 13 degrees to get a natural draping curve, while noting the belly bulge in front could also affect how the cloth rests.

Working out the front panel's plane now with top and bottom z-coordinates and a tilt direction so it sags inward toward the thighs, then mirroring the logic for the back panel using analogous but mirrored z-values and tilt direction to keep the drape symmetric.

For the back cloth I'm deciding to leave it plain, without the emblem, just a border, and sizing it slightly wider than the front panel. Then I'm moving to the pauldron geometry, working out the dome radius and shoulder placement so it properly covers the shoulder joint and arm top, factoring in the hemisphere's angular extent to find where its lower edge sits.

I'm checking the apex height against the head and beard positions to make sure the oversized pauldron (fitting the Warcraft aesthetic) doesn't clip into the beard or head geometry, since they occupy different z-depths, and I'm tilting the pauldron outward by 25 degrees before starting on the second lame plate beneath it.

Then for the lower lames, I'm stacking two smaller cylindrical segments down the upper arm with slightly decreasing radii, tinted steel with gold rim accents, tilted outward to match the arm's angle, and aligning the shoulder joint center with the plate center before moving on to the radial gold rib detailing on the main pauldron.

I'll settle on treating the rim band as painted near v<0.1, accepting some risk it lands near the apex instead. I'm also considering adding a small gold spike/cone detail on top of the pauldron dome for a fancier Warcraft-style look.
